summary: 14 days of CGM data show average glucose 122 mg/dL with time-in-range 86%, but notable overnight hypoglycemia (time-below-range up to 18.5% in early morning) and occasional severe lows (as low as 41 mg/dL). Afternoon hyperglycemia is present but cannot be analyzed without meal records. The profile basal of 0.6 U/h from midnight appears too strong, and the max IOB limit of 25 U removes a critical safety constraint, allowing dangerous insulin stacking. No carbohydrate entries exist, making all meal-related assessments impossible. A planned conservative sequence: reduce overnight basal, then lower the max IOB limit, then introduce consistent meal logging to enable future CR and ISF review.

analysis_steps.findings: CGM coverage is 98.7% with a 5-minute cadence and only 10 gaps (max 65 minutes), providing reliable trend analysis. 655 insulin records are present, but zero carb or meal bolus entries exist, making any meal-driven assessment unreliable. AAPS profile is declared as authoritative for the period.

analysis_steps.findings: Multiple severe hypoglycemic events (lowest 41 mg/dL on 14-Aug, 42 mg/dL on 21-Aug) and time-below-range >5% on several days. Overnight lows cluster in local hours 0-3 with TBR up to 18.5%. Afternoon hyperglycemia reaches TAR 32.1% at 16:00. GLP-1 use may contribute to sensitivity but is not the sole driver.

analysis_steps.findings: Overnight basal 0.6 U/h from 00:00-05:00 likely drives hypoglycemia in early morning hours (TBR up to 18.5%) despite glucose averaging near target. Afternoon basal 0.5 U/h may be too low but cannot be separated from meal effects. Target segments are clinically appropriate.

analysis_steps.data_gaps: Daytime hyperglycemia could be due to insufficient bolusing rather than basal, so afternoon basal adjustment not yet supported.

analysis_steps.findings: Static ISF of 56 mg/dL/U is irrelevant in practice because dynamic ISF overrides it (variable_sens ranges 27.8-178.7). DIA=10 h is long but cannot be adequately assessed without meal data. Carb ratios cannot be evaluated. No changes recommended.

analysis_steps.findings: The max IOB limit of 25 U is a critical safety gap, allowing dangerous insulin stacking with no practical bound. Observed IOB peaks of 5.9 U, combined with dynamic ISF amplification, contribute to severe lows. Dynamic ISF is active but likely compensating for an overly aggressive overnight basal; changing the adjustment factor now is premature. Other safety limits (max basal) are acceptable.

analysis_steps.findings: The strongest and most actionable finding is overnight hypoglycemia driven by the 00:00 basal rate of 0.6 U/h. A reduction to 0.5 U/h is the priority change. The unsafe 25 U max IOB limit must be reduced after basal adjustment to avoid confounding effects. Meal logging is essential before any CR, ISF, or DIA changes. All other profile and AAPS settings should remain unchanged until post-change data and meal records are available.

strengths: Overall time-in-range of 86.0% indicates reasonably good glucose management.
CGM coverage is high (98.7%) with consistent 5-minute cadence, providing reliable trend data.
AAPS SMB/UAM configuration is well set up and not contributing to safety issues.
Dynamic ISF is active and likely provides adaptive sensitivity compensation.
issues: Recurrent overnight hypoglycemia, especially between midnight and 3 a.m., with time-below-range exceeding 18% and severe lows down to 41 mg/dL.
Max IOB limit of 25 U removes a critical safety barrier, enabling dangerous insulin stacking and contributing to severe hypoglycemia.
Complete absence of carbohydrate logging prevents any meal-related assessment or optimization of carb ratios, ISF, DIA, and prebolus strategy.
Daytime hyperglycemia (afternoon/evening) cannot be differentiated between basal deficit and under-bolusing.

recommendations.title: Reduce overnight basal rate to reduce hypoglycemia
recommendations.description: The basal rate from 00:00 to 05:00 of 0.6 U/h appears too strong, contributing to frequent early-morning lows. Reducing it will lower hypoglycemia risk while maintaining basal coverage. Monitor overnight glucose for 3-5 days and adjust further if needed.

recommendations.title: Lower max IOB to a safe value
recommendations.description: The current max IOB of 25 U is dangerously high; observed IOB peaks of ~6 U already cause severe lows. A lower limit (e.g., 5 U) will prevent excessive insulin stacking and improve overall safety. This change should follow basal adjustment to avoid confounding.

recommendations.title: Start consistent carbohydrate logging
recommendations.description: No meal data exists, preventing any analysis of CR, ISF, DIA, or prebolus timing. Begin logging all meals (time and grams) and boluses immediately to enable future reviews.

suggested_change.suggested_value: active logging of carbohydrates and meal boluses

profile_recommendation.recommendation: Reduce the basal rate from 00:00 to 05:00 from 0.6 U/h to 0.5 U/h. Verify overnight glucose stability over at least 3 nights before considering further adjustments.
profile_recommendation.rationale: Hourly local glucose data show repeated hypoglycemia in the early morning hours (TBR up to 18.5%) despite near-target averages, indicating the basal rate exceeds fasting needs. A conservative reduction to 0.5 U/h addresses the most likely cause of lows without abolishing needed background insulin.
profile_recommendation.next_check: Review overnight sensor glucose after 3 nights with the new basal rate. If time-below-range remains >5% or severe lows recur, further reduction to 0.45 U/h may be considered.

parameter_decisions.rationale: Overnight hypoglycemia correlates strongly with this basal period; hourly glucose data shows excessive insulin action. Reducing to 0.5 U/h balances safety and basal needs. Further adjustment will depend on post-change monitoring.

parameter_decisions.parameter: AAPS / max basal and max IOB limits
parameter_decisions.rationale: The max IOB of 25 U is a clear safety hazard, allowing extreme insulin stacking. Reducing it to 5 U aligns with observed safe IOB peaks and will prevent severe hypoglycemia. The max basal rate (12 U/h) is excessive but rarely used; keeping it unchanged for now.
Dynamic ISF appears to be compensating for an overly aggressive basal. Changing the factor now could worsen control. Keep and reassess after basal and IOB adjustments.
No carb data to evaluate these; keeping default values is appropriate until meal logging is established.

meal_strategy_summary.suggestion: Start logging all carbohydrate intakes (time and estimated grams) and corresponding meal boluses in Nightscout. Until reliable meal data exists, SMB/UAM will handle meal rises reactively, which may cause unpredictable excursions. Prebolus timing, immediate bolus percentage, CR, ISF, and extended carb strategies cannot be recommended.
meal_strategy_summary.rationale: Zero carb entries prevent any analysis of meal-related glucose patterns. The system's ability to control postprandial spikes depends on accurate meal declarations.
meal_strategy_summary.next_observation: Once at least 3 days of consistent meal logs are available, review postprandial glucose profiles to begin evaluating CR and ISF.

implementation_steps: Adjust the basal rate from 00:00 to 05:00 to 0.5 U/h. Monitor overnight glucose for 3-5 nights and confirm reduction in time-below-range.

After basal change is verified, lower the max IOB limit from 25 U to 5 U to prevent insulin stacking. Monitor for adequate correction of hyperglycemia; if needed, increase gradually but not above 8 U.
Begin logging all carbohydrate consumption and meal boluses immediately. This is essential before any further profile adjustments.
After 1-2 weeks of steady basal/IOB and consistent meal logs, re-run analysis to evaluate carb ratios, ISF, and DIA.
Do not change any other profile or AAPS settings in parallel; make changes one at a time and evaluate each for 3-5 days.
education: Overnight basal rates often need to be slightly below daytime needs due to lower insulin requirements during sleep.
Max IOB should be set to a value that limits total active insulin to a safe multiple of basal, preventing dangerous stacking.
Dynamic ISF adapts to changing sensitivity but cannot compensate for fundamentally incorrect basal rates.
Meal logging is the foundation of any AAPS optimization; without it, CR and ISF cannot be accurately tuned.
safety_notes: All proposed changes are decision-support only. The user must independently verify, change one setting at a time, and closely monitor glucose.
Severe hypoglycemia risk is real; keep fast-acting carbohydrates available, especially during the first nights after basal adjustment.
Discuss any changes with a healthcare provider before implementing.
Do not adjust multiple insulin delivery settings simultaneously; observe the effect of each change for several days before proceeding.
